Primary.text: What is the capital city of Scotland?
Primary.explanation: Edinburgh is Scotland's capital, home to Edinburgh Castle.

Primary.text: What is the capital city of Wales?
Primary.explanation: Cardiff is the capital city of Wales.

Primary.text: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
Primary.explanation: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.

Primary.text: How many countries make up the United Kingdom?
Primary.explanation: The UK is England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Primary.text: Thomas is puffing north. Which direction is behind him?
Primary.explanation: South is the opposite of north.

Primary.text: In which direction does the Sun rise in the morning?
Primary.explanation: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west.

Primary.text: In which direction does the Sun set in the evening?
Primary.explanation: The Sun sets in the west.

Primary.text: Which direction is halfway between north and east?
Primary.explanation: North-east lies halfway between north and east.

Primary.text: On a map, what is the box that explains what the symbols mean called?
Primary.explanation: A map's key (or legend) tells you what each symbol means.

Primary.text: On most maps, which colour is used to show rivers, lakes and seas?
Primary.explanation: Mapmakers use blue for water.

Primary.text: What is the capital city of France?
Primary.explanation: Paris is the capital of France.

Primary.text: What is the capital city of Italy?
Primary.explanation: Rome is the capital of Italy.

Primary.text: What is the capital city of Japan?
Primary.explanation: Tokyo is the capital of Japan.

Primary.text: What is the capital city of Ireland, across the Irish Sea from Sodor?
Primary.explanation: Dublin is the capital of the Republic of Ireland.

Primary.text: In which city would you find the Eiffel Tower?
Primary.explanation: The Eiffel Tower stands in Paris, France.

Primary.text: In which country would you find the Great Wall?
Primary.explanation: The Great Wall stretches across northern China.

Primary.text: In which country are the ancient Pyramids of Giza?
Primary.explanation: The Pyramids of Giza are near Cairo in Egypt.

Primary.text: In which city is the Statue of Liberty?
Primary.explanation: The Statue of Liberty stands in New York Harbor.

Primary.text: In which country is the Sydney Opera House?
Primary.explanation: The Sydney Opera House is in Sydney, Australia.

Primary.text: In which country would you find the Taj Mahal?
Primary.explanation: The Taj Mahal is in Agra, India.

Primary.text: What is an island?
Primary.explanation: An island, like Sodor, has water all around it.

Primary.text: Which island lies in the Irish Sea, not far from Sodor?
Primary.explanation: The Isle of Man sits in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland.

Primary.text: What is the Sahara?
Primary.explanation: The Sahara in North Africa is the largest hot desert in the world.

Primary.text: Which animal is well suited to living in the hot, dry desert?
Primary.explanation: Camels can go a long time without drinking water.

Primary.text: Polar bears live in which cold place?
Primary.explanation: Polar bears live around the Arctic, near the North Pole.

Primary.text: What is a mountain that can erupt with hot lava called?
Primary.explanation: Volcanoes can erupt with lava, ash and gas.

Primary.text: What is the longest river in the United Kingdom?
Primary.explanation: The River Severn flows through Wales and England.

Primary.text: What is the highest mountain in Wales?
Primary.explanation: Snowdon, or Yr Wyddfa, is the highest mountain in Wales.

Primary.text: What is the highest mountain in England, in the Lake District?
Primary.explanation: Scafell Pike in Cumbria is England's highest peak.

Primary.text: In which season do many trees lose their leaves?
Primary.explanation: Leaves change colour and fall in autumn.

Primary.text: Which instrument measures how hot or cold it is?
Primary.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature.

Primary.text: Which instrument collects and measures rainfall?
Primary.explanation: A rain gauge collects rain so it can be measured.

Primary.text: Which tool shows which way the wind is blowing?
Primary.explanation: A weather vane points to show the wind's direction.

Primary.text: What do you often see in the sky when the Sun shines during rain?
Primary.explanation: Sunlight shining through raindrops makes a rainbow.

Primary.text: In the UK, which season has the shortest days and longest nights?
Primary.explanation: Winter days are short and nights are long.

Primary.text: What is a large area of land thickly covered with trees called?
Primary.explanation: A forest is a big area full of trees.

Primary.text: Which is the hottest and wettest kind of forest, found near the equator?
Primary.explanation: Tropical rainforests are hot and rainy all year.

Primary.text: What do we call the place where a river flows into the sea?
Primary.explanation: A river's mouth is where it meets the sea.

Primary.text: Which ocean lies between Europe and North America?
Primary.explanation: The Atlantic Ocean separates Europe and Africa from the Americas.

Primary.text: What is the capital city of Spain?
Primary.explanation: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

Secondary.text: Lines of latitude run in which direction around the globe?
Secondary.explanation: Lines of latitude (parallels) run east–west, measuring distance north or south of the equator.

Secondary.text: What is the latitude of the North Pole?
Secondary.explanation: The North Pole is at 90 degrees north.

Secondary.text: What is the name of the line of latitude at about 23.5° north of the equator?
Secondary.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer lies about 23.5° north.

Secondary.text: The Tropic of Capricorn lies in which hemisphere?
Secondary.explanation: The Tropic of Capricorn is about 23.5° south of the equator.

Secondary.text: Lines of longitude meet at which two points?
Secondary.explanation: All meridians converge at the poles.

Secondary.text: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours. How many degrees of longitude make roughly one hour of time difference?
Secondary.explanation: 360° divided by 24 hours is 15° per hour.

Secondary.text: If you travel east across time zones, what usually happens to local clock time?
Secondary.explanation: Places to the east see the Sun rise earlier, so their clocks are ahead.

Secondary.text: Crossing which line changes the calendar date by one day?
Secondary.explanation: The International Date Line roughly follows 180° longitude.

Secondary.text: What was the name of the supercontinent that existed about 300 million years ago?
Secondary.explanation: Pangaea later broke apart into today's continents.

Secondary.text: The Himalayas formed mainly because which two plates collided?
Secondary.explanation: The Indian Plate pushing into the Eurasian Plate built the Himalayas.

Secondary.text: What do we call molten rock once it has erupted onto the Earth's surface?
Secondary.explanation: Molten rock is magma underground and lava at the surface.

Secondary.text: The point on the Earth's surface directly above where an earthquake starts is called the...
Secondary.explanation: The epicentre lies directly above the focus (hypocentre).

Secondary.text: The zone of many volcanoes and earthquakes around the edge of the Pacific Ocean is called the...
Secondary.explanation: The Ring of Fire follows plate boundaries around the Pacific.

Secondary.text: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, what are the tectonic plates doing?
Secondary.explanation: It is a divergent boundary where new crust forms.

Secondary.text: A giant sea wave caused by an undersea earthquake is called a...
Secondary.explanation: Undersea earthquakes can displace water and create tsunamis.

Secondary.text: In the water cycle, what is the process of water vapour cooling to form clouds?
Secondary.explanation: Condensation turns water vapour into tiny droplets that form clouds.

Secondary.text: Water vapour released from plant leaves is called...
Secondary.explanation: Plants lose water through their leaves by transpiration.

Secondary.text: Rain, snow, sleet and hail are all forms of...
Secondary.explanation: Precipitation is any water falling from clouds.

Secondary.text: Where does a river begin?
Secondary.explanation: A river's source is its starting point, often in hills or mountains.

Secondary.text: A smaller river that joins a larger one is called a...
Secondary.explanation: Tributaries feed water into the main river.

Secondary.text: When a meander is cut off from the main river, what landform is created?
Secondary.explanation: Erosion and deposition cut off the loop, leaving an oxbow lake.

Secondary.text: A delta forms at a river mouth mainly because of...
Secondary.explanation: The river slows as it enters the sea and drops its sediment.

Secondary.text: The wide, tidal mouth of a river where fresh water meets sea water is called an...
Secondary.explanation: Estuaries are where rivers meet the tide.

Secondary.text: Which climate has hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters?
Secondary.explanation: Mediterranean climates are found around the Mediterranean Sea and similar regions.

Secondary.text: Which cold, treeless biome has permanently frozen ground called permafrost?
Secondary.explanation: Tundra has permafrost and very few trees.

Secondary.text: Which biome is tropical grassland with scattered trees, like much of East Africa?
Secondary.explanation: Savannas have grasses, scattered trees and a wet and dry season.

Secondary.text: What does 'climate' describe?
Secondary.explanation: Climate is the long-term pattern of weather, usually over 30 years or more.

Secondary.text: Waves hurling sand and pebbles against a cliff to wear it away is called...
Secondary.explanation: Abrasion is erosion by material scraping against rock.

Secondary.text: The movement of sand and shingle along a coastline by waves is called...
Secondary.explanation: Waves hitting the beach at an angle move material along the coast.

Secondary.text: On a map with a scale of 1:50,000, what does 1 cm on the map represent?
Secondary.explanation: 50,000 cm equals 500 metres.

Secondary.text: On a map of Sodor's hills, contour lines very close together show...
Secondary.explanation: Close contours mean the height changes quickly.

Secondary.text: When giving a grid reference, which do you read first?
Secondary.explanation: Remember 'along the corridor, then up the stairs': eastings first.

Secondary.text: What is the capital city of Canada?
Secondary.explanation: Ottawa, in Ontario, is Canada's capital.

Secondary.text: What is the capital city of Australia?
Secondary.explanation: Canberra was purpose-built as Australia's capital.

Secondary.text: What is the capital city of Brazil?
Secondary.explanation: Brasília became Brazil's capital in 1960.

Secondary.text: What is the capital city of Turkey?
Secondary.explanation: Ankara, not Istanbul, is Turkey's capital.

Secondary.text: Which mountain range runs down the western side of South America?
Secondary.explanation: The Andes stretch along South America's west coast.

Secondary.text: The Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, is in which country mainly?
Secondary.explanation: The Atacama Desert lies mostly in northern Chile.

Secondary.text: Which river flows through Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade?
Secondary.explanation: The Danube flows through many central and eastern European capitals.

Secondary.text: Iceland uses heat from underground rocks to make electricity. What is this energy called?
Secondary.explanation: Geothermal energy uses the Earth's internal heat.
